REAL ESTATE AGENCY RELATIONSHIP DISCLOSURE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA · Pat T. Alvarez

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law on the disclosure of real estate agency relationships in a transaction involving the real property at 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA, where Pat T. Alvarez is named as seller and Jordan T. Reyes is named as buyer. It states what California law provides about the kinds of agency relationships a real estate agent may have in a real property transaction — seller's agent, buyer's agent, or dual agent — and about the disclosures the law requires concerning those relationships. It is separate from, and in addition to, any Transfer Disclosure Statement, HOA/CC&R disclosure, or lead-based paint disclosure provided in connection with this transaction, each of which concerns different subject matter. This information sheet does not itself identify, establish, or confirm which agency relationship exists in this transaction, and it does not tell Pat T. Alvarez, Jordan T. Reyes, or any real estate agent involved what agency relationship to choose or how to proceed.

WHAT KINDS OF PROPERTY AND TRANSACTIONS THIS DISCLOSURE LAW COVERS
The statutes governing agency-relationship disclosure define "real property," for purposes of that disclosure duty, to include not only single-family residential property but also multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, commercial real property, vacant land, a ground lease coupled with improvements, and certain manufactured or mobile homes sold through an agent. "Real property transaction" is defined broadly as any transaction for the sale of real property in which a buyer, a seller, or both retain an agent, including a listing or an offer to purchase. Within that broader scope, "single-family residential property" is itself a defined term that reaches beyond a simple one-to-four-unit house: it includes real property improved with one to four dwelling units, a unit in a residential stock cooperative, condominium, or planned unit development, and certain mobilehomes or manufactured homes sold through a real estate broker. A separate and narrower statute in this same article — the broker's duty to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection and disclose what it would reveal — is expressly limited to a prospective buyer of residential real property improved with one to four dwelling units or a qualifying manufactured home; that narrower unit-count trigger belongs to that separate visual-inspection duty, not to the agency-relationship disclosure and confirmation duties described elsewhere in this information sheet.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Real property” means any estate specified by subdivision (1) or (2) of Section 761 in property, and includes (1) single-family residential property, (2) multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, (3) commercial real property, (4) vacant land, (5) a ground lease coupled with improvements, or (6) a manufactured home as defined in Section 18007 of the Health and Safety Code, or a mobilehome as defined in Section 18008 of the Health and Safety Code, when offered for sale or sold through an agent pursuant to the authority contained in Section 10131.6 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(j), California Civil Code, definition of "real property" for agency-disclosure purposes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "“Real property transaction” means a transaction for the sale of real property in which an agent is retained by a buyer, seller, or both a buyer and seller to act in that transaction, and includes a listing or an offer to purchase."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(k), California Civil Code, definition of "real property transaction" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "“Single-family residential property” or “single-family residential real property” means any of the following: (1) Real property improved with one to four dwelling units, including a leasehold exceeding one year’s duration. (2) A unit in a residential stock cooperative, condominium, or planned unit development."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(l), California Civil Code, definition of "single-family residential property" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "It is the duty of a real estate broker or salesperson, licensed under Division 4 (commencing with Section 10000) of the Business and Professions Code, to a prospective buyer of residential real property improved with one to four dwelling units or a manufactured home as defined in Section 18007 of the Health and Safety Code, to conduct a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection of the property offered for sale and to disclose to that prospective buyer all facts materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that an investigation would reveal, if that broker has a written contract with the seller to find or obtain a buyer or is a broker who acts in cooperation with that broker to find and obtain a buyer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079(a), California Civil Code, separate one-to-four-unit visual-inspection duty (contrast only) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.)

The agency-relationship disclosure and confirmation duties described in this document are not limited to a sale of residential real property comprising one to four dwelling units — that unit-count trigger applies to a different, narrower duty (the broker's visual-inspection duty) codified in a separate section of the same article, quoted here only for contrast. The three citations to § 2079.13 below are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the citation to § 2079 is an independent section addressing a different duty, included to show the contrast in scope rather than to corroborate the § 2079.13 definitions. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which scope definition applies to any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

SELLER'S AGENT, BUYER'S AGENT, AND DUAL AGENT — STATUTORY DEFINITIONS
California statutory law recognizes three distinct agency roles a real estate agent can occupy in a real property transaction. A seller's agent is a person who has obtained a listing of real property to act as agent for compensation. A buyer's agent is an agent who represents a buyer in a real property transaction. A dual agent is an agent acting, either directly or through a salesperson or broker associate, as agent for both the seller and the buyer in the same real property transaction. An agent may lawfully act as a dual agent, but only with the knowledge and consent of both the seller and the buyer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Seller’s agent” means a person who has obtained a listing of real property to act as an agent for compensation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(f), California Civil Code, definition of "seller's agent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "“Buyer’s agent” means an agent who represents a buyer in a real property transaction."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(o), California Civil Code, definition of "buyer's agent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "“Dual agent” means an agent acting, either directly or through a salesperson or broker associate, as agent for both the seller and the buyer in a real property transaction."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.13(d), California Civil Code, definition of "dual agent" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.13.)
  "A real estate agent, either acting directly or through one or more salespersons and broker associates, can legally be the agent of both the Seller and the Buyer in a transaction, but only with the knowledge and consent of both the Seller and the Buyer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, statutory disclosure form text on dual agency consent (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines these three agency roles — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. The three citations to § 2079.13 below are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the citation to § 2079.16 is an independent, separately enacted section used as a second, distinct source for the dual-agency consent requirement. This document is informational only: it does not itself identify which of these three roles any specific agent occupies in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

WHEN THE GENERAL AGENCY DISCLOSURE FORM MUST BE GIVEN
California statutory law fixes when the general agency-relationship disclosure form must be provided, and to whom, and the timing differs by which agent is providing it. A seller's agent, if any, must provide the disclosure form to the seller before entering into the listing agreement with the seller — not merely "as soon as practicable" before an offer. A buyer's agent must provide the disclosure form to the buyer as soon as practicable, before execution of a buyer-broker representation agreement and before execution of the buyer's offer to purchase; if the buyer's agent did not prepare the offer to purchase, that agent must present the disclosure form to the buyer no later than the next business day after receiving the offer from the buyer. Whichever agent provides the disclosure form must obtain a signed acknowledgment of its receipt from the buyer or seller, subject to a statutory exception.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The seller’s agent, if any, shall provide the disclosure form to the seller before entering into the listing agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.14(a)(1), California Civil Code, seller's agent disclosure timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.14.)
  "The buyer’s agent shall provide the disclosure form to the buyer as soon as practicable before execution of a buyer-broker representation agreement and execution of the buyer’s offer to purchase. If the offer to purchase is not prepared by the buyer’s agent, the buyer’s agent shall present the disclosure form to the buyer not later than the next business day after receiving the offer to purchase from the buyer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.14(a)(2), California Civil Code, buyer's agent disclosure timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.14.)
  "The agent providing the disclosure form specified in Section 2079.16 shall obtain a signed acknowledgment of receipt from the buyer or seller except as provided in Section 2079.15."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.14(b), California Civil Code, signed acknowledgment of receipt required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.14.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's timing rule for this disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. The three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.14) and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The statutory exception to the signed-acknowledgment requirement, referenced in subdivision (b) as "except as provided in Section 2079.15," is noted but not itself researched or quoted in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether the disclosure form was, or was not, timely provided or acknowledged in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described here require.

REQUIRED TEXT OF THE AGENCY DISCLOSURE FORM — DUTIES DESCRIBED
California statutory law prescribes the actual text that must appear on the general agency-relationship disclosure form, captioned "Disclosure Regarding Real Estate Agency Relationship (As required by the Civil Code)." That prescribed text separates two kinds of duty. A seller's agent owes the seller a fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty — a duty owed only to the agent's own client. A buyer's agent owes that same fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty to the buyer only. Separately, the same prescribed text describes duties that a seller's agent or a buyer's agent owes to both the buyer and the seller — including the non-client party, who is not that agent's fiduciary client: diligent exercise of reasonable skill and care in performance of the agent's duties; a duty of honest and fair dealing and good faith; and a duty to disclose all facts known to the agent materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that are not known to, or within the diligent attention and observation of, the parties. In a dual agency, the prescribed text states that the agent owes the fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty to both the seller and the buyer at once, while also providing that a dual agent may not, without the express permission of the respective party, disclose to the other party confidential information such as either party's financial position, motivations, bargaining position, or willingness to accept a lower or pay a higher price than currently offered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "DISCLOSURE REGARDING REAL ESTATE AGENCY RELATIONSHIP (As required by the Civil Code)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, prescribed disclosure form caption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  "To the Seller: A fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty in dealings with the Seller."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, seller's agent fiduciary duty to seller (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  "To the Buyer: A fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty in dealings with the Buyer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, buyer's agent fiduciary duty to buyer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  "(a) Diligent exercise of reasonable skill and care in performance of the agent’s duties. (b) A duty of honest and fair dealing and good faith. (c) A duty to disclose all facts known to the agent materially affecting the value or desirability of the property that are not known to, or within the diligent attention and observation of, the parties."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, duties owed to both parties (including the non-client) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  "In representing both Seller and Buyer, a dual agent may not, without the express permission of the respective party, disclose to the other party confidential information, including, but not limited to, facts relating to either the Buyer’s or Seller’s financial position, motivations, bargaining position, or other personal information that may impact price, including the Seller’s willingness to accept a price less than the listing price or the Buyer’s willingness to pay a price greater than the price offered."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.16, California Civil Code, dual agent's confidentiality limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.16.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's prescribed agency-disclosure form text — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction; other states use different disclosure forms or none at all. All five citations below quote different portions of the same statutory section (§ 2079.16), and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which of these duties applies to any specific agent in any specific transaction, and it does not satisfy the statute's requirement that this actual prescribed form — not this information sheet — be delivered and acknowledged.

CONFIRMING THE ACTUAL AGENCY RELATIONSHIP, IN WRITING
Separate from the general disclosure form describing the possible kinds of agency relationship, California statutory law requires the agent's actual relationship in a specific transaction to be confirmed in writing. As soon as practicable, the buyer's agent must disclose to both the buyer and the seller whether that agent is acting as the buyer's agent or as a dual agent representing both; this relationship must then be confirmed in the purchase-and-sale contract itself, or in a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller, the buyer, and the buyer's agent, prior to or coincident with execution of that contract by the buyer and seller. As soon as practicable, the seller's agent must likewise disclose to the seller whether that agent is acting as the seller's agent or as a dual agent, confirmed in the contract or a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller and the seller's agent, prior to or coincident with the seller's execution of the contract. The statute prescribes a specific checkbox form for this confirmation, under which each named agent's brokerage and license number is identified as representing the seller, the buyer, or both as a dual agent. This confirmation requirement is in addition to — not a substitute for — the general disclosure form described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "As soon as practicable, the buyer’s agent shall disclose to the buyer and seller whether the agent is acting in the real property transaction as the buyer’s agent, or as a dual agent representing both the buyer and the seller. This relationship shall be confirmed in the contract to purchase and sell real property or in a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller, the buyer, and the buyer’s agent prior to or coincident with execution of that contract by the buyer and the seller, respectively."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.17(a), California Civil Code, buyer's agent confirmation duty and timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.17.)
  "As soon as practicable, the seller’s agent shall disclose to the seller whether the seller’s agent is acting in the real property transaction as the seller’s agent, or as a dual agent representing both the buyer and seller. This relationship shall be confirmed in the contract to purchase and sell real property or in a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller and the seller’s agent prior to or coincident with the execution of that contract by the seller."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.17(b), California Civil Code, seller's agent confirmation duty and timing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.17.)
  "is the broker of (check one): [ ]the seller; or [ ]both the buyer and seller. (dual agent)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.17(c), California Civil Code, prescribed checkbox confirmation form (excerpt) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.17.)
  "The disclosures and confirmation required by this section shall be in addition to the disclosure required by Section 2079.14."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.17(d), California Civil Code, confirmation is additional to the general disclosure form (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.17.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's confirmation requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. The four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.17) and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself confirm, execute, or acknowledge any agent's actual role in this or any other transaction, and it does not satisfy the written confirmation that this statute requires — that confirmation must appear in the actual purchase contract or a separate signed writing meeting the statutory form, not in this information sheet.

THIS ARTICLE DOES NOT REDUCE AN AGENT'S OTHER DUTIES OR LIABILITY
California statutory law specifies that the agency-disclosure and confirmation requirements described in this document do not diminish an agent's duty of disclosure to buyers and sellers, and do not relieve an agent — or that agent's associate licensees, subagents, or employees — from liability for conduct connected with acts this body of law governs, including any breach of a fiduciary duty or a duty of disclosure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Nothing in this article shall be construed to either diminish the duty of disclosure owed buyers and sellers by agents and their associate licensees, subagents, and employees or to relieve agents and their associate licensees, subagents, and employees from liability for their conduct in connection with acts governed by this article or for any breach of a fiduciary duty or a duty of disclosure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.24, California Civil Code, other duties and liability not diminished (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=2079.24.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's approach to preserving other disclosure duties and liability alongside the agency-disclosure requirements described elsewhere in this document — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. Only one statutory section is cited here, so the same-section corroboration issue noted in this document's other authority clauses does not apply to this clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any agent's conduct in any specific transaction breached a fiduciary duty or a duty of disclosure, and it does not satisfy any disclosure or confirmation that the statutes described in this document require.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF REVIEW
This information sheet, describing California statutory law on agency-relationship disclosure for the real property at 456 Meadowbrook Lane, Riverside, CA, has been reviewed by the parties named below. This acknowledgment confirms only that this information sheet was reviewed. It is not the general agency disclosure form described in California Civil Code § 2079.16, and it is not the written confirmation of an actual agency relationship described in California Civil Code § 2079.17; neither of those statutory documents is satisfied by this signature block, and each must be completed separately if California law requires it for this transaction.

In a dual agency, the prescribed text states that the agent owes the fiduciary duty of utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty to both the seller and the buyer at once, while also providing that a dual agent may not, without the express permission of the respective party, disclose to the other party confidential information such as either party's financial position, motivations, bargaining position, or willingness to accept a lower or pay a higher price than currently offered.

As soon as practicable, the buyer's agent must disclose to both the buyer and the seller whether that agent is acting as the buyer's agent or as a dual agent representing both; this relationship must then be confirmed in the purchase-and-sale contract itself, or in a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller, the buyer, and the buyer's agent, prior to or coincident with execution of that contract by the buyer and seller. The statute prescribes a specific checkbox form for this confirmation, under which each named agent's brokerage and license number is identified as representing the seller, the buyer, or both as a dual agent. This confirmation requirement is in addition to — not a substitute for — the general disclosure form described elsewhere in this document.
